author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The French government says it is implementing an emergency plan to improve conditions in the education system after weeks of high school protests that have spread across France and now include universities.

Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler saw police charge towards protesters, who had built barricades with bins and fences, and break them up, with some fires and smoke in the street.

The prime minister wants to end the unrest, promising an emergency plan to address some of the students’ concerns, with more teachers a priority. But some young people who gathered at Bastille Square said they no longer trust the government. Student Mohamed Bensouna called it a revolution, saying they love France but not the government.

Finding more funds for education will be difficult as the country’s debt crisis grows.

Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reports from Paris.

description: Britain has downgraded its diplomatic presence in occupied East Jerusalem after reaching a last-minute agreement with Israel to keep its nearly 200-year-old consular building open as a smaller mission. Twenty British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving, while seven will remain at what is now known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem. Israel had ordered the consulate to close in response to Britain’s decision to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which the UK says are illegal under international law. Protesters waved Palestinian flags and scarves and called for a free Palestine. The rally began in front of the new Israeli embassy in Bogota. President Abelardo de la Espriella has restored diplomatic and commercial relations with Israel and plans to open a Colombian embassy in Jerusalem in two weeks.

Despite the relatively low turnout, there was a big presence of security forces, including anti-riot police. De la Espriella is also announcing new protest rules that would allow police to intervene with force when they feel threatened or public property is at risk.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The World Health Organization says it is investigating reports that a worker has died, and another has been infected, after being accidentally exposed to plague at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. Russia is under pressure to provide answers after lab technician Darya Shipilova, 28, died last week.

Initial media reports suggested her death was caused by pneumonic plague, contracted from a broken test tube, forcing hundreds into quarantine. 

The Kremlin has refuted the reports, with spokesperson Dmitry Peskov calling most of it false. Russia's health watchdog says there is no risk of an epidemic and that Shipilova died of pneumonia of unknown origin.

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization has requested more information on the lab tests and public health measures, and is seeking verification of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. He said the WHO lacks the full picture and cannot yet conduct a full risk assessment.

Al Jazeera's Juli
title: WHO seeks answers as Russia denies plague after Siberian lab worker's death

Protesters have gathered outside Spain's parliament in Madrid to mourn Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her lifelong home made her the face of Spain's housing crisis. She died weeks after being evicted.

Abascal was evicted from her Madrid home in September, where she had lived for more than seven decades. Her eviction sparked demonstrations across the country, turning one woman's struggle into a wider fight over soaring rents, evictions and access to housing.

The protests have put pressure on Spain's government. Housing measures were rejected in parliament last week, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has since called a snap election for November 29, putting housing at the centre of the political debate.

Al Jazeera's Dalya Al Masri reports from Madrid.

description:
Voters in London's Holborn and St Pancras head to the polls on Thursday in a by-election triggered by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer giving up his seat. 

It is the first ballot-box test for Andy Burnham, nearly three months into his premiership, and has become a tight two-horse race between the governing Labour Party and the Green Party.

The constituency is densely packed, with about 112,000 people in 10.5 square kilometres. Its residents are young, with a median age of 32, and 45 percent were born outside the UK. Three quarters rent their homes and 70 percent of households have no car.

Labour's candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, came to London from Somalia as a child refugee and became the first black woman to lead the local council. The Greens, led nationally by Zack Polanski, won some council seats from Labour in local elections, but are mired in a controversy over a conference motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, which has split the party over accusations of antisemitism.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, becoming its 201st and 202nd recipients. The Nobel Committee said they were recognised for discovering non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

It is perhaps not a particularly well-known field, and neither chemist was widely tipped for the prize. The committee described the reactions they developed as spectacular, but the question now is why they are important.

A member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, Andrei Chabes, said the work is already used to make some pharmaceuticals, including asthma medicines and antiviral drugs. More importantly, he said, it shows how to design more efficient reactions to produce such medicines, essentially a new way of manipulating chemical reactions.

Al Jazeera's Paul Rhys reports from Stockholm.
